purpose: Published throughput figures for predicting how slow a grounded question would be on hardware nobody here has.
how_to_read_this: Every row is a figure somebody else measured and published, not a figure measured here. Each one names the page it came from, the day it was read off that page, and the software that produced it.

The software matters as much as the machine. One source below publishes two columns side by side: mainline llama.cpp and ik_llama.cpp, a fork whose purpose is faster processor inference. Every figure taken from that page here is the mainline llama.cpp column. An earlier version of this table took the fork's column and labelled it llama.cpp, which inflated the processor figures by up to five times and led to a wrong conclusion about which half of the wait dominates. Engine choice is the single largest source of variance in these numbers, which is why it is named in each row rather than assumed.

A row is 'estimated' because it describes hardware this project has never run on. It becomes 'measured' only for the machine that runs 'archiv model calibrate --local', and that measurement is written into the archive, never back into this file.

Prompt reading and answer generation are kept apart because they have different bottlenecks and different remedies. Which of the two dominates is not a fixed property of Archiv: it depends on the machine and on how long an answer is wanted. See the note on the M2 Max processor row.

The band on each figure is the spread the source itself published. Where a source published a bare number with no spread, the band is that number twice and the basis says so. That is not a range, it is one observation, and a reader should treat it as one.
what_this_table_does_not_contain: Memory bandwidth. The prediction code can derive a second, independent throughput ceiling from a machine's memory bandwidth and the size of the model file, and that arithmetic is implemented and tested. No row carries a bandwidth figure, because the vendor pages that publish them are unreachable from the environment this table was built in, and a bandwidth number recalled from memory is not a cited number. Until a row has one, its prediction rests on one anchor and says so.

Any figure for Archiv's own prompt sizes. Every source below benchmarks a 512-token prompt because that is what the standard harness does. Archiv's prompts are larger, and prompt reading is not perfectly linear in prompt length, so these figures are an anchor rather than a direct answer.

Matched thread counts. On the processor-only rows the source measured prompt reading and generation at different thread counts, and each figure's basis says which. A prediction adding the two together is therefore adding measurements from two different configurations of the same machine.

profiles.note: This is the row that shows which half of the wait dominates is a property of the machine, not of Archiv. Here prompt reading runs at 54 tokens a second and generation at 14 -- a ratio of about 4. On the Ryzen row below the same ratio is about 30. So for a 1,400-token prompt, prompt reading dominates on this machine for any answer shorter than about 360 tokens, and on the Ryzen only for answers shorter than about 50.
